cards.title: What is a **stored-program computer**?
cards.body:
A computer that keeps its program in memory as numbers, in the same way it keeps its data.

Instead of being rewired for each job, the machine reads its instructions from memory one after another. To change what it does, you change the numbers in memory, not the hardware.

Why it matters: This is why firmware can be updated. A new program is just new bytes written into the chip's flash memory, and a program can be loaded, copied and checked like any other data.

Example: Flashing new firmware onto a microcontroller writes the new program's bytes into its flash. The processor itself is unchanged.

cards.title: What is an **instruction set architecture** (ISA)?
cards.body:
The contract between hardware and software: the instructions, registers and memory behavior that a program can rely on, without knowing how the chip is built inside.

Compilers target the ISA and chip designers implement it. Any processor that implements the same RISC-V base ISA can run the same machine code, whether it is a tiny slow core or a large fast one.

Why it matters: The contract lets software and hardware change independently. A faster chip that implements the same ISA runs old programs unchanged.

Watch out: The ISA says what each instruction does, not how fast it runs or how the chip is built. How a particular chip implements the ISA is called its **microarchitecture**.

cards.title: What is the **program counter** (PC)?
cards.body:
A register that holds the address of the next instruction to run.

After each instruction the PC normally moves on to the following one. In RISC-V's base integer ISA (RV32I, named on a later card) every instruction is 4 bytes long, so the PC advances by 4. Branches and jumps work by writing a different address into the PC.

Example: If the PC holds `0x00000100`, the instruction at that address runs next and the PC then becomes `0x00000104`.

Watch out: In RISC-V the PC is not one of the 32 general registers x0 to x31, so ordinary instructions cannot name it as an operand.

cards.title: What happens in the **fetch–decode–execute cycle**, and which parts of the processor take part?
cards.body:
Fetch the instruction at the address in the PC, decode it, execute it using the register file, ALU and memory, then update the PC and repeat.

- Fetch: the PC addresses memory and the instruction word comes back.
- Decode: work out which operation is requested and which registers it names.
- Execute: the **register file** (the small, fast set of registers) supplies operands, the ALU computes, memory is read or written by loads and stores, and the result is written back to a register.

Key idea: A processor is a machine that repeats this one loop for as long as it has power. A program is only a long list of things for the loop to do.

Why it matters: Every later topic, pipelines and caches included, is a way to run this same loop faster.

cards.title: What is **RV32I**, and how many integer registers does it give a program?
cards.body:
RISC-V's base integer instruction set with 32-bit registers: 32 integer registers, x0 to x31, each 32 bits wide.

The name reads RV (RISC-V), 32 (register width in bits) and I (integer). It has a few dozen simple instructions: arithmetic, logic, shifts, loads and stores, branches and jumps. It has no multiply or divide; those come from the optional M extension.

Why it matters: RV32I is small enough to implement in a very small chip and still complete enough to run compiled C.

Example: The register file holds $32 \times 32 = 1024$ bits, which is 128 bytes.

cards.title: Why is it false that you can keep a value in register `x0`, as you can in `x5`?
cards.body:
`x0` is hard-wired to zero: reading it always gives 0 and writing to it is ignored.

Example: After `addi x0, x0, 5` (add 5 to x0 and write the sum to x0), register `x0` still holds 0. The instruction `add x9, x0, x6` (x9 = x0 + x6) copies x6 into x9, because adding zero changes nothing.

Why: A constant zero is very useful. It lets one `add` or `addi` do the work of a move or of loading a small constant, lets you compare against zero, and lets you throw a result away by writing it to `x0`. It also costs no storage, so only 31 registers are real storage.

Watch out: Count only x1 to x31 when you plan how many values fit in registers.

cards.title:
In RISC-V, `addi rd, rs1, imm` adds the constant `imm` to register `rs1`, `add rd, rs1, rs2` adds two registers, and `sub rd, rs1, rs2` computes rs1 − rs2. All registers start at 0. What do x7 and x8 hold afterwards?

```asm
addi x5, x0, 6
addi x6, x0, 7
add  x7, x5, x6
sub  x8, x7, x5
```
cards.body:
x7 = 13 and x8 = 7.

Trace it line by line. `addi x5, x0, 6` adds 6 to zero, so x5 = 6. Likewise x6 = 7. Then x7 = 6 + 7 = 13, and x8 = 13 − 6 = 7.

Key idea: The 6 and 7 are **immediates**: constants stored inside the instruction itself. Adding one to `x0` is how RISC-V puts a small constant into a register.

Watch out: `sub` subtracts its third operand from its second, so `sub x8, x7, x5` is x7 − x5, not x5 − x7.

cards.title:
A toolchain turns one C statement into the three forms below. Which tool produces line 2 from line 1, and which produces line 3 from line 2?

```asm
1.  y = x + 5;
2.  addi x5, x6, 5
3.  0x00530293
```
cards.body:
The compiler turns line 1 into line 2; the assembler turns line 2 into line 3, which is machine code.

The compiler chooses instructions and registers (here it kept y in x5 and x as x6). Line 2 is assembly text, which people can read. The **assembler** translates that text, almost mechanically, into the bits the processor executes. Those bits are called **machine code**; line 3 shows one 32-bit instruction in hexadecimal.

Why: Seeing all three forms explains why you read assembly to check what the compiler did, and why a disassembler can turn machine code back into text.

Watch out: People often say "compile" for the whole chain. The linker then joins the object files into an executable.

cards.title: You must choose an instruction-set style for a tiny, low-power microcontroller core. **RISC** (few, simple, equal-length instructions) or **CISC** (many, complex, variable-length instructions)?
cards.body:
RISC: simple, regular instructions keep the decoder and the whole core small, cheap and easy to speed up, at the price of somewhat more instructions per program.

RISC stands for reduced instruction set computer; RISC-V and Arm are RISC-style. Most RISC instructions do one small thing, and arithmetic works only on registers.

The other side: **CISC** (complex instruction set computer, x86 being the best known) lets one instruction do more, such as read memory and add in one step. Programs need fewer, denser instructions, but instruction lengths vary and decoding is harder.

Watch out: The comparison depends on conditions. Large modern x86 chips translate their complex instructions into simple internal steps, so the gap that matters is mostly in small, low-power cores.

cards.title: What is **assembly language**?
cards.body:
A human-readable text form of machine code: one line per instruction, written as a short name (the mnemonic) followed by its operands.

Example: `add x7, x5, x6` means "put x5 + x6 into x7". For most arithmetic instructions the first operand is the destination and the sources follow.

Labels such as `loop:` name addresses so you never count bytes by hand, and a `#` starts a comment.

Why it matters: Assembly is the lowest level people can comfortably read, and it is what you inspect to see what the compiler produced.

Watch out: Assembly belongs to one ISA. RISC-V and Arm assembly look different even for the same C code.

cards.title: RISC-V memory is **byte addressed**. How is the **effective address** of `lw x5, 8(x10)` computed, and how far apart are consecutive 32-bit words?
cards.body:
Effective address = x10 + 8 (base register plus offset), and consecutive 32-bit words are 4 bytes apart.

Byte addressing means each address names one byte. A word is 4 bytes, so word number $k$ of an array that starts at address $b$ is at $b + 4k$. The offset is a signed 12-bit immediate.

Example: With x10 = `0x1000`, `lw x5, 8(x10)` reads the 4 bytes at `0x1008` to `0x100B`, which is the third word.

Watch out: The load reads address x10 + 8. It does not read address 8, and it does not multiply anything by 4. Word loads expect an address that is a multiple of 4 (alignment); an unaligned one may fault or run slowly.

cards.title:
All registers start at 0. What do x7 and x8 hold afterwards, as decimal numbers?

```asm
addi x5, x0, 12
addi x6, x0, 10
and  x7, x5, x6
or   x8, x5, x6
```
cards.body:
x7 = 8 and x8 = 14.

Write the values in binary: $12 = 1100_2$ and $10 = 1010_2$. A bit of `and` is 1 only where both inputs have a 1: $1000_2 = 8$. A bit of `or` is 1 where either has a 1: $1110_2 = 14$.

Why: `and`, `or` and `xor` work on every bit independently, exactly like `&`, `|` and `^` in C. `andi`, `ori` and `xori` do the same with an immediate.

Watch out: These are bitwise operations, not the logical `&&` and `||` of C.

cards.title:
x5 starts at −16. What do x6, x7 and x8 hold afterwards?

```asm
addi x5, x0, -16
slli x6, x5, 2
srai x7, x5, 2
srli x8, x5, 28
```
cards.body:
x6 = −64, x7 = −4, x8 = 15.

−16 is `0xFFFFFFF0` in 32-bit two's complement. `slli` shifts left by 2, which multiplies by 4: −64. `srai` is an arithmetic shift right, which copies the sign bit into the vacated bits: −4. `srli` is a logical shift right, which fills with zeros: `0xFFFFFFF0 >> 28 = 0xF = 15`.

Why it matters: A left shift by $k$ multiplies by $2^k$, which is how compilers scale array indexes.

Watch out: Use `srai` for signed values and `srli` for unsigned ones. A logical shift of a negative number gives a large positive number.

cards.title:
Memory holds the 32-bit word 30 at address `0x1004` and the word 12 at `0x1008`, and x10 = `0x1000`. After this code runs, which address holds which value?

```asm
lw  x5, 4(x10)
lw  x6, 8(x10)
add x7, x5, x6
sw  x7, 12(x10)
```
cards.body:
The word at address `0x100C` becomes 42.

**Load word** (`lw`) copies 4 bytes from memory into a register; **store word** (`sw`) copies a register into 4 bytes of memory. The effective addresses are `0x1004`, `0x1008` and `0x100C`. The two loads fetch 30 and 12, `add` makes 42, and `sw` writes it.

Example: In C this is `p[3] = p[1] + p[2];` with `int *p = (int *)0x1000;`.

Key idea: Arithmetic happens only on registers. Memory is touched only by loads and stores.

Watch out: In `sw x7, 12(x10)` the register is the value being stored. In `lw` the register is the destination.

cards.title:
The byte at address `0x2000` is `0xF0` and x10 = `0x2000`. What do x5 and x6 hold afterwards, as 32-bit hex?

```asm
lb  x5, 0(x10)
lbu x6, 0(x10)
```
cards.body:
x5 = `0xFFFFFFF0` and x6 = `0x000000F0`.

`lb` loads a byte and sign-extends it: bit 7 is copied into the upper 24 bits, so `0xF0` becomes −16. `lbu` (load byte unsigned) zero-extends it, giving 240.

Why it matters: Use `lb` for `int8_t` and signed char data, and `lbu` for `uint8_t` data such as sensor bytes. Picking the wrong one turns 240 into −16.

Watch out: There is a `sb` (store byte) that writes the low 8 bits, but no `sbu`: a store needs no extension.

cards.title: What is a **pseudo-instruction**, and what do `li`, `mv` and `j` expand to?
cards.body:
An assembler shorthand that expands to one or more real instructions: `li x5, 100` is `addi x5, x0, 100`, `mv x5, x6` is `addi x5, x6, 0`, and `j label` is `jal x0, label`.

`jal` jumps to a label and saves the return address in its first register; using `x0` throws that address away, so it is a plain jump. Other examples are `nop` (`addi x0, x0, 0`) and `ret` (a return from a function, covered in the function-call unit).

Why it matters: Pseudo-instructions keep assembly readable while the processor only needs the small real set.

Watch out: A disassembler may show the real instruction rather than your pseudo name, and instruction counts always count real instructions. A large `li` can expand to two instructions.

cards.title:
Fill in the blank so the code does `if (a == b) c = 1; else c = 2;` with `a` in x5, `b` in x6 and `c` in x7.

```asm
       ____ x5, x6, Lelse
       addi x7, x0, 1
       j    Lend
Lelse: addi x7, x0, 2
Lend:  # code continues
```

`bne`

A **branch** instruction tests a condition and, if it is true, jumps to a label; otherwise execution falls through to the next instruction. RISC-V has `beq`, `bne`, `blt`, `bge`, `bltu` and `bgeu`.

To skip the "then" part when `a != b`, the code must test the opposite of the C condition. The `j Lend` is a **jump**, which always goes to its target; it keeps the "then" part from running into the "else" part.

Watch out: Compilers usually invert the C condition, so `if (a == b)` becomes `bne`. Leaving out `j Lend` makes the code run both branches.

cards.title:
x5 holds n = 4. What is in x6 when execution reaches `done`?

```asm
      addi x6, x0, 0
      addi x7, x0, 1
loop: blt  x5, x7, done
      add  x6, x6, x7
      addi x7, x7, 1
      j    loop
done:
```
cards.body:
10, which is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4.

This is `s = 0; for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) s += i;`. The `blt x5, x7, done` instruction branches when x5 < x7, that is when n < i, so the loop exits once i exceeds n. The `j loop` at the bottom is an unconditional jump back to the test.

Example: For n = 4 the body runs for i = 1, 2, 3, 4 and the `blt` test runs 5 times.

Watch out: The exit test is the opposite of the loop condition `i <= n`, which is why it reads n < i. Swapping the operands would exit at once.

cards.title:
x10 = `0x1000` holds the base of an `int` array {5, −2, 7, −9, 0} and x11 = 5 is its length. The program counts the negative elements in x6. What is x6 at `done`, and how many instructions execute from the first line up to and including the branch to `done`?

```asm
      addi x6, x0, 0
      addi x7, x0, 0
loop: bge  x7, x11, done
      slli x5, x7, 2
      add  x5, x10, x5
      lw   x8, 0(x5)
      bge  x8, x0, skip
      addi x6, x6, 1
skip: addi x7, x7, 1
      j    loop
done:
```
cards.body:
x6 = 2, and 40 instructions execute.

The C version is `count = 0; for (i = 0; i < n; i++) if (a[i] < 0) count++;`. The `bge x8, x0, skip` branch skips the increment when the element is not negative, so 5, 7 and 0 are skipped and −2 and −9 are counted. Zero is not negative, so it is not counted.

Counting instructions: 2 setup instructions. A non-negative element runs 7 (`bge`, `slli`, `add`, `lw`, `bge`, `addi`, `j`), and a negative one runs 8 because of the extra `addi`. That is $2 + 3 \times 7 + 2 \times 8 = 39$, plus the final `bge` that exits, giving 40.

Why it matters: The instruction count is the first factor of the performance equation in a later unit.

cards.title: What is a **calling convention**, and how does it relate to the **application binary interface** (ABI)?
cards.body:
A calling convention is the agreed set of rules for passing arguments, returning results and preserving registers across a function call. It is the core of the ABI, the binary-level contract between separately compiled pieces of code.

In the RISC-V integer convention the first arguments go in `a0` to `a7` (x10 to x17), the result comes back in `a0` (and `a1`), `ra` is x1, `sp` is x2, `t0` to `t6` are temporaries and `s0` to `s11` are saved registers.

Why it matters: Code compiled separately, by different compilers or written by hand, can only call each other if everyone follows the same rules.

Watch out: Names like `a0` come from the ABI. The hardware only knows x10.

cards.title: What is a **caller-saved register** in the RISC-V calling convention, and which registers are they?
cards.body:
A register that a called function may overwrite freely, so the caller must save any value it still needs before making the call. In RISC-V these are `a0` to `a7`, `t0` to `t6` and `ra`.

Example: A function keeps a count in `t0` and then calls `f`. After `f` returns, `t0` may hold anything. The caller must store it on the stack before the call, or keep it in an s register.

Key idea: Caller-saved means "don't count on it surviving a call".

Tip: Use t registers for short-lived values that are not needed across a call, since they cost nothing to use.

cards.title: What is a **callee-saved register** in the RISC-V calling convention, and which registers are they?
cards.body:
A register that a called function must return exactly as it found it. In RISC-V these are `s0` to `s11` and `sp`.

A function that wants to use `s0` must save the old value when it starts, usually on the stack, and restore it before returning.

Example: A loop in a caller keeps its counter in `s1` across many calls. It needs no saving around each call, because every callee that uses `s1` restores it.

Watch out: Choose by lifetime. A value needed after a call belongs in an s register (callee-saved) or on the stack; a short temporary belongs in a t register.

cards.title: How do `jal` and `jalr` implement a function call and return, and what does the **return address** register `ra` hold?
cards.body:
`jal ra, f` saves the address of the next instruction in `ra` and jumps to `f`; `jalr x0, 0(ra)` (written `ret`) jumps back to the address in `ra`.

Example: A `jal ra, func` at address `0x100` with `func` at `0x200` sets `ra = 0x104` and the PC to `0x200`. The later `ret` sets the PC to `0x104`.

`jalr rd, offset(rs1)` jumps to the address in `rs1` plus the offset, so it can also jump through a function pointer. Writing `x0` as the destination throws the link away.

Watch out: There is only one `ra`. A function that calls another function overwrites its own return address unless it saves `ra` first.

cards.title:
This fragment sits inside a function that has already saved its own `ra`. Why can it compute the wrong sum if `f` is compiled separately and uses `t0` internally?

```asm
    jal  ra, f
    add  a0, a0, t0    # f's result + 5
```

`t0` is caller-saved, so `f` may overwrite it; the caller must save it before the call and restore it after.

A fix that follows the convention:

```asm
    li   t0, 5
    addi sp, sp, -16
    sw   t0, 12(sp)
    jal  ra, f
    lw   t0, 12(sp)
    addi sp, sp, 16
    add  a0, a0, t0
```

Keeping the 5 in `s1` instead also works, but then the function must save and restore `s1` for its own caller.

Watch out: The bug depends on the body of `f`. It can pass tests while `f` is tiny and break when `f` is rewritten to use more temporaries.

A caller puts −3 in `a0` and −8 in `a1`, then runs `jal ra, max2`. What is in `a0` when `max2` returns? (`max2` is a **leaf function**: it calls no other function.)

```asm
max2: bge a0, a1, done
      mv  a0, a1
done: ret
```
cards.body:
−3

The arguments arrive in `a0` and `a1` and the result leaves in `a0`. `bge` compares as signed numbers, −3 ≥ −8 is true, so it skips the `mv` and `a0` still holds −3. In C this is `int max2(int a, int b) { return a >= b ? a : b; }`.

Why: A leaf function needs no stack frame. It never overwrites `ra`, because it makes no call, and it uses no s registers, so it can end with a bare `ret`.

Watch out: `ret` is only the pseudo-instruction `jalr x0, 0(ra)`; it jumps to wherever `ra` points.

cards.title:
This function calls `helper`. Fill in the blank so that `twice_plus` returns to its own caller.

```asm
twice_plus:
    addi sp, sp, -16
    sw   ____, 12(sp)
    jal  ra, helper
    addi a0, a0, 1
    lw   ra, 12(sp)
    addi sp, sp, 16
    ret
```
cards.body:
`ra`

`jal ra, helper` overwrites `ra` with the address after the call. If `ra` is not saved in that slot, the `lw ra, 12(sp)` reloads whatever garbage was there, so `ret` jumps to a wrong address. (With no save and no reload at all, `ret` would jump back to the instruction after the `jal` and loop forever.)

The first two lines are the **prologue**: they move the **stack pointer** `sp` down (the stack grows toward lower addresses) to make a frame, and save registers in it. The last three lines are the **epilogue**: they restore `ra`, move `sp` back up and return.

Example: The C source is `int twice_plus(int x) { return helper(x) + 1; }`.

Watch out: The RISC-V ABI keeps `sp` a multiple of 16, which is why a one-word save still takes a 16-byte frame.

```asm
    sw   ra, 12(sp)
    sw   s0, 8(sp)
    mv   s0, a0
    jal  ra, g
    add  a0, a0, s0
    lw   s0, 8(sp)
    lw   ra, 12(sp)
    addi sp, sp, ____
    ret
```

Two saved words need only 8 bytes, but the frame size is rounded up to a multiple of 16, and the offsets 12 and 8 must lie inside the frame. The epilogue undoes the prologue: it restores `s0` and `ra`, then moves `sp` back by the same amount.

Why: `f` computes `g(x) + x`, so `x` must survive the call to `g`. A callee-saved register holds it, and because `f` uses `s0`, it must restore the caller's `s0` before returning.

```asm
      sw   ra, 12(sp)
      sw   a0, 8(sp)
      addi a0, a0, -1
      jal  ra, sum
      lw   t0, 8(sp)
      add  a0, a0, t0
      lw   ra, 12(sp)
      addi sp, sp, 16
```

`sp` = `0x7FD0`, with 3 frames on the stack (for n = 3, 2 and 1).

cards.title: What is an **instruction format**, and what are RV32I's six formats called?
cards.body:
The layout of an instruction's 32 bits into fields. RV32I has six formats: R, I, S, B, U and J.

The R-type layout, from bit 31 down, is `funct7` (7 bits), `rs2` (5), `rs1` (5), `funct3` (3), `rd` (5) and `opcode` (7). The **opcode** selects the instruction family; `funct3` and `funct7` pick the exact operation within it; `rd` is the destination register and `rs1` and `rs2` are the source registers.

Example: `sub x4, x5, x6` encodes as `0x40628233`.

Which format is used for what: R for register-to-register arithmetic, I for immediates, loads and `jalr`, S for stores, B for branches, U for `lui` and `auipc`, J for `jal`.

cards.title: What are **compressed instructions** (RVC) in RISC-V?
cards.body:
16-bit encodings of the most common instructions, from the C extension, mixed freely with 32-bit ones to make programs smaller.

The processor tells them apart by the lowest two bits: `11` means a 32-bit instruction, while `00`, `01` and `10` mean a 16-bit one. The assembler or compiler picks them automatically, for example with `-march=rv32imc`.

Why it matters: Smaller code needs less flash and uses the instruction fetch bandwidth better. The RISC-V designers estimate that 50 to 60 percent of the instructions in a typical program can use the 16-bit forms, which cuts code size by about 25 to 30 percent.

Watch out: Programmers see no change: same registers, same behavior. A compressed instruction is only a shorter spelling, so the PC can advance by 2 or by 4.

cards.title: Why does RISC-V keep the register fields `rs1`, `rs2` and `rd` in the same bit positions in every format that has them?
cards.body:
So the hardware can start reading the register file immediately, before it has finished working out which instruction it is.

The fields never move: `rs1` is bits 19 to 15, `rs2` is bits 24 to 20 and `rd` is bits 11 to 7. Those bits can be wired straight to the register file while the opcode is still being decoded.

The cost is that the immediate bits end up scattered around the remaining places, which is why the S and B formats split their immediates.

Example: In `add x7, x5, x6` (`0x006283B3`) and in `sw x7, 12(x10)` the `rs1` and `rs2` bits sit in the same slots.

Watch out: U and J formats have no `rs1` or `rs2`, so those bits carry immediate bits instead; only `rd` stays at bits 11 to 7.

`lui x5, 0x12346` followed by `addi x5, x5, -1`.

`lui` (load upper immediate, U-type) puts a 20-bit immediate in the upper 20 bits and zeros in the lower 12, so x5 = `0x12346000`. The `addi` immediate is sign-extended: the low 12 bits `0xFFF` are read as −1, not +4095. So $0x12346000 + (-1) = 0x12345FFF$.

Rule: the upper part is $(\text{value} + 0x800) \gg 12$, which rounds up whenever bit 11 of the value is set.

cards.title: What is **cycles per instruction** (CPI)?
cards.body:
The average number of clock cycles a processor needs to complete one instruction: total cycles divided by instructions executed.

Example: A program that takes 1,200 cycles to execute 1,000 instructions has CPI = 1.2.

A single-cycle design has CPI = 1 by construction. Stalls push CPI above 1, and a processor that finishes several instructions per cycle has CPI below 1.

Watch out: CPI depends on the program as well as the chip, because loads, branches and other instructions cost different numbers of cycles. Always say which program a CPI was measured on.

cards.title: How are the **clock period** and the **clock frequency** of a processor related?
cards.body:
$T_{clk} = 1/f$: the period is the time of one clock cycle, and the frequency is the number of cycles per second.

Example: At 100 MHz the period is 10 ns. At 2 GHz it is 0.5 ns, which is 500 ps.

Why it matters: The period must be at least as long as the slowest path between flip-flops (the critical path). A faster clock therefore means shortening the longest path.

Watch out: Keep units consistent. Convert MHz to Hz, or ns to s, before dividing.

cards.title: State the **Iron Law of performance** for the execution time of a program.
cards.body:
$T = \mathrm{IC} \times \mathrm{CPI} \times T_{clk}$, which is instructions executed times cycles per instruction times seconds per cycle.

The units cancel: instructions × (cycles/instruction) × (seconds/cycle) = seconds. Equivalently $T = \mathrm{IC} \times \mathrm{CPI} / f$.

Example: 2,000,000 instructions at CPI 1.5 and 100 MHz take $2\times10^6 \times 1.5 / 10^8 = 0.03$ s, which is 30 ms.

Key idea: Every speedup must lower at least one of the three factors. If one factor improves while another gets worse, only the product tells you the result.

cards.title: Which factor of the Iron Law does each layer mostly control: the compiler and ISA, the microarchitecture, and the circuit technology?
cards.body:
The compiler and ISA mainly set the instruction count, the microarchitecture mainly sets CPI, and circuit design and process technology mainly set the clock period.

Example: Compiling with optimization usually lowers the instruction count. A better memory system lowers CPI by cutting stalls. A newer manufacturing process shortens the period.

Watch out: The factors interact. Splitting the work into shorter steps shortens the clock period but can add stall cycles, which raises CPI a little. A design is better only if the product of the three gets smaller.

cards.title: Why is it false that a processor with a higher clock frequency, or a higher MIPS rating, always runs the same program faster?
cards.body:
Because time is IC × CPI × $T_{clk}$: a higher clock can come with a higher CPI or more instructions, and MIPS ignores how much work each instruction does.

MIPS means millions of instructions per second, which is $f / (\mathrm{CPI} \times 10^6)$. It counts instructions, but the same program needs different numbers of instructions on different ISAs and compilers.

Example: A core with no hardware multiply may need dozens of simple instructions for one multiplication. Its MIPS rating can look as good as a core with a multiply instruction while it takes much longer on multiply-heavy code.

Tip: Compare processors by the measured execution time of your own workload.

Y is faster: 22 ms against 25 ms, a speedup of about 1.14.

The **speedup** of Y over X is $T_X / T_Y = 25/22 \approx 1.14$. A speedup above 1 means the new design is faster.

Key idea: Y has the lower clock yet wins, because its lower CPI more than makes up for the slower clock.

cards.title: State **Amdahl's law**: if a fraction $p$ of the original execution time is sped up by a factor $s$, what is the overall speedup?
cards.body:
$S = \dfrac{1}{(1-p) + p/s}$

The new time, as a fraction of the old, is the untouched part $(1-p)$ plus the improved part $p/s$. Speedup is old time divided by new time.

As $s \to \infty$ the speedup approaches $1/(1-p)$. With $p = 0.8$ the ceiling is 5, however fast the improved part becomes.

Watch out: $p$ is the fraction of run time, not of the lines of code or of the instructions, so profile first.

Key idea: Improving one part makes the rest the bottleneck.

cards.title: What is the **datapath** of a processor?
cards.body:
The hardware that moves and transforms data for instructions: the PC, instruction memory, register file, ALU, data memory, and the multiplexers and wires that join them.

The **instruction memory** holds the program and the **data memory** holds variables. Textbook designs draw them as two blocks so an instruction can be fetched and data accessed in the same cycle; real chips often reach one memory through separate caches or paths.

Key idea: The datapath is the muscle and the control unit, on the next card, is the brain that steers it.

Example: For `add`, data flows from the register file through the ALU and back to the register file. For `lw` it also passes through data memory.

cards.title: What do the **control unit** and its **control signals** (RegWrite, MemWrite, ALUSrc, ResultSrc, Branch) do in a single-cycle RISC-V processor?
cards.body:
The control unit reads the instruction's opcode and funct fields and sets control signals that steer the datapath's multiplexers and enable its writes.

- `RegWrite`: write the result into the register file at the clock edge.
- `MemWrite`: write a register value into data memory.
- `ALUSrc`: the ALU's second operand comes from a register (0) or from the immediate (1).
- `ResultSrc`: what goes back to the register file, the ALU result or the data read from memory.
- `Branch`: this is a branch, so the PC takes the branch target if the ALU says the condition holds.

Why it matters: Each instruction type is just a different setting of these signals. The control unit is plain combinational logic of the opcode.

cards.title: What does the **immediate extender** do in the datapath?
cards.body:
It picks the immediate bits out of the instruction according to its format and sign-extends them to 32 bits for the ALU or the PC.

The immediate bits sit in different places in the I, S, B, U and J formats, so a control signal (often called `ImmSrc`) tells the extender which format to use. Sign extension copies the sign bit, bit 31 of the instruction, into the upper bits.

Example: The 12-bit immediate of `addi x5, x6, -3` is `0xFFD`. The extender turns it into `0xFFFFFFFD`.

Watch out: Branch and jump immediates have an implicit bit 0 equal to 0, since targets are multiples of 2, and the extender inserts it.

cards.title: How does the **register file** of a single-cycle RISC-V core read and write registers in one cycle?
cards.body:
It has two read ports that act like combinational logic, always showing the registers named by `rs1` and `rs2`, and one write port that stores the new value of `rd` on the clock edge when `RegWrite` is 1.

Reads are not clocked: put the register numbers in and the values come out after a delay. Writes happen only at the clock edge, at the end of the cycle.

Example: `add x5, x5, x6` reads the old x5 and x6, the ALU adds them during the cycle, and the clock edge then stores the sum in x5.

Why it matters: Two read ports are needed because most instructions have two source operands. Register x0 is wired so that it always reads 0 and ignores writes.

cards.title: In a **single-cycle processor**, why does the slowest instruction (usually `lw`) set the clock period for every instruction?
cards.body:
Every instruction gets exactly one clock cycle, so the period must cover the longest path through the datapath, which is the path of `lw`.

A single-cycle processor finishes each instruction in one cycle, so its CPI is 1. The `lw` path runs through instruction memory, register file, ALU, data memory and back to the register file. `add` and `beq` skip data memory but still wait for the same long clock.

Why it matters: The slack of fast instructions is wasted. This is the main motivation for pipelining, which lets the clock follow a short stage instead of the whole instruction.

Key idea: This is the critical path rule from digital logic applied to a whole processor.

4. Data memory is read at that address, since `MemWrite` = 0.

cards.title: A tiny always-on sensor controller needs only a few MHz and must be as small as possible. A **single-cycle** or a **pipelined** core?

Why: Pipeline registers add area and power, and hazards add control logic. If the required instruction rate is modest, that cost buys nothing.

cards.title: What is a **pipeline** in a processor, and what are the five classic stages of a RISC-V pipeline?
cards.body:
A pipeline splits instruction execution into **stages** so that several instructions are in progress at once, one per stage. The five stages are IF (instruction fetch), ID (decode and register read), EX (execute), MEM (memory access) and WB (write back).

Example: While instruction 1 is in EX, instruction 2 is in ID and instruction 3 is in IF.

Registers between the stages hold each instruction's values as it moves along, and every stage does its work in one clock cycle.

Key idea: It is an assembly line. Each instruction still visits every station, but all the stations are busy at the same time.

cards.title: Why does pipelining raise **throughput** but not the **latency** of a single instruction?
cards.body:
Each instruction still passes through all the stages, so its latency stays the same or grows slightly, but a new instruction finishes every cycle, so more instructions finish per second.

Throughput is instructions completed per second; latency is the time one instruction takes from start to finish.

Example: Suppose the single-cycle core takes 800 ps per instruction. A five-stage version with a 300 ps clock needs $5 \times 300 = 1500$ ps for one instruction, which is worse, yet it finishes one instruction every 300 ps instead of every 800 ps.

Watch out: Pipelining speeds up a long stream of instructions. It does nothing for one lone instruction.

cards.title: What is a pipeline **hazard**, and what are the three kinds?
cards.body:
A situation where the next instruction cannot safely go ahead in its normal cycle. The kinds are structural (a resource conflict), data (a result is not ready yet) and control (the next instruction is not yet known).

- Structural: two instructions need the same hardware in the same cycle, such as one memory used for both fetch and data access.
- Data: `sub x6, x5, x9` right after `add x5, x7, x8` needs x5 before `add` has written it.

cards.title: What is **forwarding** (bypassing) in a pipeline?
cards.body:
Sending an instruction's result straight from the pipeline register where it has just been produced to the input of a later instruction's EX stage, without waiting for it to be written back to the register file.

Without forwarding, an instruction right behind an `add` that needs its result would wait 2 cycles, since the register file is written in WB. With forwarding the sum, ready at the end of EX, is needed only at the start of the next instruction's EX, so there is no stall.

The hardware is a multiplexer at each ALU input and comparators that check whether a source register matches an older instruction's destination.

Why it matters: Forwarding keeps CPI near 1 for back-to-back dependent ALU instructions.

cards.title: Why can't forwarding remove every data hazard? What is a **load-use hazard**, and what does the pipeline do about it?
cards.body:
A load's data is not available until the end of MEM, too late for the next instruction's EX in the following cycle, so the pipeline inserts one **stall** (a **bubble**) even with forwarding.

A stall holds the dependent instruction and those behind it for one cycle while an empty slot passes down the pipeline. After the stall the loaded value is forwarded.

Example: `lw x5, 0(x10)` followed by `add x6, x5, x7` costs one stall. If an independent instruction sits between them, the stall disappears.

Tip: Compilers schedule an independent instruction after each load to hide this stall.

cards.title:
Which pairs of instructions have a data hazard (a later instruction reads a register an earlier one writes), and how many stall cycles does a five-stage pipeline with full forwarding need?

```asm

sub x8, x5, x9
and x10, x5, x8
or  x11, x12, x13
```
cards.body:
`sub` depends on `add` (x5), and `and` depends on `add` (x5) and on `sub` (x8); `or` is independent. With forwarding there are no stalls.

All three dependences are on ALU results, which can be forwarded from the end of EX or MEM to the next EX, so no cycle is lost. Without forwarding, `sub` would have to wait 2 cycles for `add` to reach WB.

Watch out: A dependence only matters while the two instructions overlap in the pipeline. An instruction three or more places after the writer finds the value already in the register file.

On a classic five-stage pipeline with full forwarding, how many clock cycles pass from the first instruction's fetch (cycle 1) until the last instruction finishes write-back?

```asm
lw  x5, 0(x10)
add x6, x5, x7
sub x8, x6, x9
```
cards.body:
8 cycles: 7 for three independent instructions ($3 + 4$), plus 1 stall for the load-use hazard.

```text
      1  2  3  4  5  6  7  8
lw    IF ID EX ME WB
add      IF ID ID EX ME WB
sub         IF IF ID EX ME WB
```

`add` needs x5 in its EX stage, but `lw` only produces it at the end of ME in cycle 4, so `add` repeats ID in cycle 4 and executes in cycle 5. `sub` is held in IF for the same cycle. `sub` gets x6 forwarded from `add`'s EX, so no further stall occurs.

Key idea: Without the hazard the last write-back would be in cycle 7.

cards.title: A branch's outcome is not known until EX, so the pipeline must guess. For a small low-power core with a short pipeline, is **static** prediction (a fixed rule such as "backward branches taken, forward branches not taken") or **dynamic** prediction (a table of past outcomes) the better choice?
cards.body:
Static: its rule is nearly free in area and power, and a wrong guess on a short pipeline costs only a cycle or two. Dynamic prediction wins when the pipeline is deep and each misprediction is expensive.

**Branch prediction** guesses the outcome and fetches along the guessed path. A right guess costs nothing. A wrong guess forces a **pipeline flush**: the wrongly fetched instructions are discarded and fetch restarts. In a classic five-stage pipeline that resolves branches in EX, the penalty is 2 cycles.

Why: The static rule works because loop branches jump backward and are usually taken. A dynamic predictor needs storage, update logic and power, which is a poor deal when the penalty is small.

What is the effective CPI?
cards.body:
1.22

Effective CPI is the ideal CPI plus the average stall cycles per instruction:

$\mathrm{CPI} = 1 + 0.25 \times 0.40 \times 1 + 0.20 \times 0.30 \times 2 = 1 + 0.10 + 0.12 = 1.22$

Load-use stalls add 0.10 cycles per instruction and branch flushes add 0.12.

Why it matters: This feeds the Iron Law: with the same instruction count and clock, the program runs 22% slower than the ideal pipeline.

Watch out: Weight each penalty by how often the event happens per instruction. Do not apply the stall to all loads or all branches.

cards.title: What are **temporal locality** and **spatial locality**?
cards.body:
Temporal locality: an item used recently is likely to be used again soon. Spatial locality: items near a recently used address are likely to be used soon.

Example: A loop counter and an accumulator show temporal locality, since they are touched on every iteration. Scanning an array in order shows spatial locality.

Why it matters: Caches exploit both. They keep recently used data (temporal) and fetch a whole line at a time (spatial), so most accesses find their data nearby.

Watch out: Chasing the pointers of a linked list scatters accesses across memory and has poor spatial locality.

cards.title: Roughly how long does one access take at each level of a typical processor's memory hierarchy: L1 cache, DRAM, SSD (flash) and spinning disk?
cards.body:
About 1 ns for an L1 SRAM cache, 50 to 100 ns for DRAM, 10 to 100 µs for an SSD and several ms for a spinning disk.

Each step down the **memory hierarchy** is slower by roughly 50 to 1000 times, and also larger and cheaper per byte. (SRAM is the fast memory used for caches; DRAM is the denser, slower main memory.) Locality is what lets the whole hierarchy behave like a large and fast memory.

Example: Energy follows the same pattern. Horowitz (ISSCC 2014, 45 nm) gives about 5 pJ for a 32-bit read from an 8 KB SRAM and about 640 pJ for a DRAM read, roughly 130 times more.

Watch out: These are order-of-magnitude figures for desktop-class systems. A microcontroller reads its on-chip SRAM in about one cycle, and its flash may need extra wait states at high clock rates.

cards.title: What is a **cache line** (block), and what are a **cache hit** and a **cache miss**?
cards.body:
A cache line is the fixed-size chunk of memory (commonly 32 or 64 bytes) that moves in and out of a cache as one unit. A hit finds the requested data in the cache; a miss does not, and the whole line must be fetched from the next level.

The miss rate is misses divided by accesses, and the hit rate is 1 minus the miss rate.

Example: A 64-byte line holds 16 four-byte ints. Reading `a[0]` misses and brings in the line, and `a[1]` to `a[15]` then hit.

Why it matters: Fetching whole lines is how a cache turns spatial locality into hits.

cards.title: What is a **direct-mapped cache**?
cards.body:
A cache where each memory line can be stored in exactly one cache line, chosen by the address: index = block number mod number of cache lines.

The block number is the address divided by the line size. A lookup checks only one place, so it is simple, fast and cheap.

Example: A cache with 4 lines of 16 bytes sends addresses `0x00` and `0x40` to the same line, because $\lfloor 0x40/16 \rfloor = 4$ and $4 \bmod 4 = 0$.

Watch out: Two frequently used blocks that map to the same line keep evicting each other, even while other lines sit empty.

cards.title: How is a memory address split into **tag**, **index** and **offset** for a cache, and what does each field do?
cards.body:
The offset (low bits) picks the byte within the line, the index (middle bits) picks the cache line or set, and the tag (high bits) is stored with the line and compared to check that it holds the right data.

Offset bits = $\log_2$(line size in bytes), index bits = $\log_2$(number of sets), and the tag is the rest of the address.

A lookup uses the index to find the line, compares the stored tag with the address's tag, and checks the line's valid bit, which says the line holds real data. A match is a hit and returns the byte at the offset.

Watch out: Tags and valid bits are extra storage. They are not counted in the cache's quoted data capacity.

cards.title: State the formula for **average memory access time** (AMAT).
cards.body:
$\mathrm{AMAT} = t_{hit} + m \times t_{penalty}$: the hit time plus the miss rate times the miss penalty.

Here $m$ is the miss rate as a fraction and $t_{penalty}$ is the extra time to fetch from the next level on a miss. Use one unit, such as cycles, for all three.

Example: A 1-cycle hit time, a 5% miss rate and a 100-cycle penalty give $1 + 0.05 \times 100 = 6$ cycles.

Watch out: Every access pays the hit time, so a change that lowers the miss rate but slows the hit time can make AMAT worse.

cards.title: A small embedded cache has room for a fixed number of lines. Which is usually the better design for general code: **direct-mapped**, or **2- to 4-way set-associative**?
cards.body:
Set-associative (2 to 4 ways) usually wins on miss rate for general code because it avoids most conflict misses; direct-mapped wins when the fastest hit time, smallest area and lowest power matter most.

In a **set-associative cache** an address maps to one set, and the set holds several lines (ways). The line can be in any way, and the tags of all ways are compared at once. When a full set takes a new line, **LRU replacement** evicts the least recently used one.

Misses come in three kinds: compulsory (first touch), capacity (the working set exceeds the cache) and conflict (too many blocks map to one set). More ways remove more conflict misses; a fully associative cache has none.

Watch out: The gain shrinks quickly beyond about 4 ways, while the comparison hardware keeps growing.

cards.body:
Write-back: repeated stores to the same line cost one memory write at eviction instead of one per store, which saves memory bandwidth and energy.

Write-back needs a dirty bit per line, and evicting a dirty line writes the whole line to memory. Until then memory is stale.

The other side: **Write-through** is simpler and keeps memory always up to date, which suits data that other masters read, such as a DMA engine (a peripheral that copies memory without the CPU) or another core, without cache maintenance. It is usually paired with a write buffer so the processor does not wait.

Watch out: With write-back, a DMA engine reading a buffer can see stale data unless software first cleans the cache.

cards.title: What is the **stride** of a memory access pattern, and how does it set the fraction of accesses that miss the cache?

Stride is the distance in bytes between consecutive accesses. With line size $L$ and stride $s < L$, about $s/L$ of the accesses miss; once $s \ge L$ every access touches a new line.

cards.title: What is the difference between a **virtual address** and a **physical address**, and what hardware translates one into the other?
cards.body:
A virtual address is what a program uses; a physical address is the actual location in memory. The **memory management unit** (MMU) translates virtual to physical on every access.

Each process gets its own virtual address space, which can start at 0 and can be larger than the installed memory. The operating system controls the mapping.

Example: Two programs may both use virtual address `0x10000`, and the MMU sends them to different physical addresses.

Watch out: On a system with an MMU, the pointer values a C program prints are virtual addresses. On a microcontroller with no MMU, a pointer is the physical address.

cards.title: What are a **page**, a **page table** and a **page table entry** (PTE)?
cards.body:
A page is a fixed-size block of memory (commonly 4 KiB) that is the unit of translation. The page table maps each virtual page number to a physical page, and each of its entries, a PTE, also holds a valid bit and permission bits.

A virtual address splits into a page number and a page offset. Translation replaces the page number and leaves the offset unchanged. With 4 KiB pages the offset is 12 bits.

Example: In a 32-bit address `0x00003ABC`, the page number is 3 and the offset is `0xABC`.

Why it matters: If the PTE's valid bit is 0, the access causes a page fault, covered on a later card.

cards.title: What is a **translation lookaside buffer** (TLB), and why is it needed?
cards.body:
A small, fast cache of recent virtual-to-physical page translations, so most accesses avoid reading the page table in memory.

Without it, every load or store would need extra memory reads to find its PTE, one for each level of the page table. On a TLB hit the translation takes about a cycle. On a TLB miss, hardware or the operating system walks the page table and then fills the TLB.

Watch out: A TLB miss is not a page fault. A TLB miss only means the translation was not cached, and the page may be in memory. A page fault means there is no valid mapping.

cards.title: What three things does virtual memory give an operating system?
cards.body:
Isolation (each process sees only its own address space), protection (permissions on each page, such as read-only or no-execute) and demand paging (pages are loaded only when first touched, so programs can use more memory than is installed).

Example: Address 0 is normally left unmapped. A null-pointer dereference then hits an invalid page, the hardware faults, and the program ends with a segmentation fault.

Key idea: The extra layer of indirection between addresses a program uses and addresses memory uses is what makes all three possible.

cards.title: What happens on a **page fault**, and why is it so much more expensive than a TLB miss?
cards.body:
The access hits a page with no valid mapping, the CPU traps (jumps) into operating-system code, and the OS either fixes the mapping (possibly reading the page from storage) or ends the process, and then the instruction is retried.

A TLB miss costs a few memory reads. A page fault runs operating-system code and may wait for storage: tens of microseconds for an SSD or milliseconds for a spinning disk, against about 100 ns for DRAM.

Causes: first touch of a page (demand paging), a page that was swapped out, a write to a read-only page, or an invalid address (which becomes a segmentation fault).

Watch out: The delay of a page fault is unpredictable, so systems with hard deadlines avoid demand paging.

cards.title: A 32-bit system uses 4 KiB pages and 4-byte PTEs, with one flat page table per process. How big is one process's page table, and how does a two-level table avoid that cost?
cards.body:
$2^{20}$ entries × 4 B = 4 MiB per process; a two-level table allocates second-level tables only for the parts of the address space actually in use.

The page offset takes 12 bits, so the page number has $32 - 12 = 20$ bits, giving $2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$ entries. At 4 bytes each that is 4 MiB, even for a tiny process, and 40 MiB for ten processes.

A two-level table splits the 20 bits into 10 + 10. The top 10 bits index a first-level table, whose entries point to second-level tables of 1024 entries (4 KiB each, exactly one page). A process uses a few regions (code, data, heap, stack), so most second-level tables never exist.

Example: RISC-V's Sv32 scheme uses this 10 + 10 + 12 split.

cards.title: A battery-powered microcontroller runs a hard real-time control loop and must stop a faulty task from overwriting the kernel's memory. Use an **MMU** or an **MPU**?
cards.body:
An MPU: the **memory protection unit** enforces access permissions on a few memory regions without translating addresses, so timing stays predictable and area and power stay small.

An MPU holds a small number of configurable regions, each with a base, a size and permissions, commonly 8 or 16 on Arm Cortex-M cores. An access that breaks the rules causes a fault. There are no page tables, no TLB misses and no page faults, so every access takes a fixed time. This is why most microcontrollers have no MMU, only an optional MPU.

The other side: Without an MMU there are no separate address spaces and no demand paging, and every task must be linked at its own physical addresses. A general-purpose OS such as Linux needs an MMU.
